new.pl: South side of Menomonie Street near Michigan Street, Shawtown, Eau Claire
new.v: Mill-hand coins and tokens, tools, buttons
new.st: Pfaff places Daniel Shaw's shingle mill in Shawtown, on the south side of Menomonie Street near Michigan Street; a photo from the 1880s shows dozens of workers and teams. Shaw came from Industry, Maine, in 1856, and the ground around his mills, with houses for managers and workers, a grist mill (Crescent Mills) and a store, came to be called Shawtown. After his mill burned in 1867 he put in sprinklers and gave fire protection to Shawtown residents. Albert Halverson lost a leg in the Shaw mill in 1872. The 1883 Sanborn map's D. S. L. Co. store and office pin is about 60 m away and the Shaw sawmill about 120 m.
new.t: A millworkers' neighborhood of the 1860s-1900s: yards, alleys and any unbuilt lots off Menomonie Street. Private and city land: ask first.
src: Pfaff, Settlement and Survival: Building Towns in the Chippewa Valley 1850-1925 (Chippewa Valley Museum, 1994), your screenshots

new.n: The 1857 Half Moon Lake log canal and the first sheer boom
new.pl: Chippewa River end of the old canal, near 9th Avenue and Menomonie Street, Eau Claire
new.v: Boom chain, spikes, pier iron, river-worker losses
new.st: In 1857 Adin Randall, Daniel Shaw, Orrin Ingram and others dug a canal about 1,200 ft long from the Chippewa River to Half Moon Lake near 9th Avenue and Menomonee Street, between the Ingram, Kennedy & Co. mill and the Valley Lumber Co., to make the lake a holding pond for logs (map by Daniel Kerntop, Pfaff p. 19). The Eau Claire Telegraph of 25 May 1857 mentions the canal and "a sheer boom thrown out some distance above the mouth." After the 1861 floods washed out the booms, James Allan and Levi Pond of Eau Claire invented the sheer boom proper here: a line of logs with angled fins that the current held in place, swung aside for steamboats with a windlass. Lumbermen around the world soon copied it. The 1883 Sanborn rafting shed pin is about 160 m west.
new.t: Look at the shoreline at the old canal mouth and for pier footings. River bank: look only where it is public land.
src: Pfaff, Settlement and Survival: Building Towns in the Chippewa Valley 1850-1925 (Chippewa Valley Museum, 1994), your screenshots
pinev: Placed where today's 9th Avenue line meets the Chippewa bank below Menomonie Street; the canal line itself is not traced yet, so good to about 150 m

new.n: Empire Lumber Co. raft-building works, west bank of the Chippewa
new.pl: West bank of the Chippewa below the east end of Menomonie Street, Eau Claire
new.v: Grub pins, raft chain, tools, coins
new.st: An 1870s photo in Pfaff shows the Empire Lumber Co. rafting works here, with rafting tables, cribs of sawn lumber and crews; KXE was Empire's log mark. Mill hands stacked lumber into 16 by 32 ft cribs pinned with grub stakes; seven cribs made a string, and four strings a "Chippewa raft." In 1887 an Eau Claire Lumber Co. raft was cut in two on a pier of the Kelsey Street bridge.
new.t: River-bank working ground: grub pins, raft chain and coins. Most of the bank is city land; check the rules first.

new.n: Olinger Gardens beer garden and dance pavilion, opposite Walter's City Brewery
new.pl: 300 block of Elm Street, Eau Claire
new.v: Coins, tokens, jewelry, bottle caps and glass
new.st: Walter's City Brewery stood at 318 Elm Street. On the opposite corner of the same block, Olinger Gardens was a favorite place for entertainment, especially for German residents: German bands played in the dance pavilion, and Sunday afternoons were for families (caption to an 1890-1910 poster, Pfaff p. 69).

new.n: "Pig Town": the millhands' neighborhood by the Eau Claire Lumber Co. mill
new.pl: North side, Eau Claire, around the Eau Claire Lumber Co. mill on the Eau Claire River
new.v: Coins, buttons, toys and household losses from worker yards
new.st: Louise Schlegelmilch remembered the poor neighborhood around the Eau Claire Lumber Company mill as "Pig Town", where "nearly everyone kept pigs, cows or chickens": Irish, Norwegian and German millhand families such as the Fitzpatricks, Olsons and Dusendofers. In the 1884 flood "logs washed up into Forest Street, on the north side," and Forest and East Madison Streets flooded. The 1883 Sanborn mill pin is about 120 m from here.
new.t: Back yards of worker houses from the 1870s-1900s. Most of it is rebuilt, so look for old lawns and alleys, with permission.

new.n: Old Music Hall, Barstow Street and Kelsey Street (now Grand Avenue), burned 1871
new.pl: Northwest corner of Barstow Street and Grand Avenue (old Kelsey Street), Eau Claire
new.st: Pfaff prints a photo of the ruin of the Old Music Hall, at the northwest corner of Barstow and Kelsey (now Grand Avenue), which burned in the 1871 fire. Nearby were the Old Star House (Gasthaus zum Stern), John Kurts' saloon, William Bowman's butcher shop and the Scandinavian House, all in the fire of 3 November 1875 (Free Press). Smith & Rowe's grocery at 114 Kelsey was lit by electric arc light in 1882.
new.t: Downtown and paved: mainly a stop for a historic walk.

new.n: "Tannery Town": the U.S. Leather Co. tannery, Stanley (1897)
new.v: Worker coins, tokens, buttons, tannery hardware
new.st: P. A. Gilbert's U.S. Leather tannery came to Stanley from Pennsylvania in 1897, drawn by the railroads and hemlock bark. It employed nearly 200 men at $1.00-1.25 a day; in 1908 it took 75,000 green hides and shipped 80 carloads of leather. Across town, the Big Four Canning Factory put up 100,000 cans a day in 1914. The Stanley, Merrill & Phillips Railway ran logging trains out of town (photo of the "Three Spot"). The Northwestern Lumber Co. moved here from Porter's Mills in the 1890s and sawed its last log in 1920.
new.t: Find the tannery lot on the 1913 Chippewa County plat or a 1938 air photo first; tannery ground can hold old chemical waste, so check before you dig. Ask the owner.

new.st: Eau Claire realtor Ben Faast's Wisconsin Colonization Co. sold the cutover land around Conrath to settlers ("Buy a Good Farm Now ... Let the Cow Show You How!"). Many were Polish; Veronica Golunki learned the polka here as a child. Of 37 farmers who bought land from the John S. Owen Lumber Co. in 1918-19, fewer than half ever got a deed (Pfaff pp. 89-91; Wisconsin Colonization Co. papers at the UW-Eau Claire archives).
new.t: Still a small hamlet: look for the abandoned farm sites around it (Abandoned farms layer), with permission. Conrath Cemetery, about 1 km away, is look-only.

new.n: Ojibwa: Ben Faast's planned cutover town
new.st: Ojibwa was Ben Faast's planned cutover community, meant to grow into a farm service town for the Wisconsin Colonization Co. Chester Korenski's Sawyer County farm was appraised in February 1924 as "Wild cut-over country ... 6 acres swamp ... Distance to Market Towns: 4 miles Ojibwa" (Pfaff pp. 89-90). The Hall-Raynor stopping place pin is about 190 m away.

d-ghost-porters-mills.st: More from Pfaff (pp. 18, 27, 73-75): the town grew around the mills of partners Gilbert E. Porter and Delos Moon. In 1873 the Northwestern Lumber Co. had 120 men making 100,000 ft of lumber, 30,000 ft of lath and 50,000 shingles a day. Forty families lived in company houses on named streets, with gardens and livestock, and single men rented on "Tenement Row." Main Street had blacksmith shops, stables, a shoe shop, a hotel and two candy stores. The Scandinavian Evangelical Lutheran church and school were built in 1885, there was a Methodist church, and the Modern Woodmen of America hall was hauled away across the ice in 1907. In 1890 the town had 1,190 people, nearly half working in the mills. When Northwestern moved to Stanley in the 1890s, residents hauled away some buildings and abandoned others (Mississippi Valley Lumberman, 24 March 1899: "Porter's Mills is gone.") Look for the church and school lots and the hall ground: the hall photo shows it on open flat ground by the river.
src: Pfaff, Settlement and Survival: Building Towns in the Chippewa Valley 1850-1925 (Chippewa Valley Museum, 1994), your screenshots

d-beef-slough.st: Pfaff (pp. 24-25): as many as 1,500 men worked the sorting works at times. In 1867 Chippewa Valley mill owners built a dam across Beef Slough "to improve navigation"; the Beef Slough backers tore it out, and in the scuffle the Beef Slough Co. secretary lost a finger and Knapp, Stout's manager at Read's Landing, Thomas B. Wilson, was jailed. In 1880 a 23-ft rise sent over 200 million board feet through the Chippewa booms in 12 hours. In 1881 Ingram and Weyerhaeuser formed the Chippewa Logging Co. ("the pool"), split 65/35 to the Mississippi side.
src: Pfaff, Settlement and Survival: Building Towns in the Chippewa Valley 1850-1925 (Chippewa Valley Museum, 1994), your screenshots

d-reads-landing.st: Orrin Ingram's 1859 raft letters start at "Reeds Landing" (15 and 17 June 1859: a gale, the river 8-10 miles wide, low water), and 1860s immigrants were put ashore here and carried up the Chippewa on the steamboat Chippewa (photo 1868) or the small boat Monitor to Durand (Pfaff pp. 22, 33-34).

d-ec-steamboat-landings.st: In 1857 the Jennie Whipple came twice a week, landing settlers opposite Reed's Hall and the Niagara House, and daily stages ran from Alma and Sparta. An 1870 photo shows the steamer Ida Campbell docked on Water Street below the Ingram, Kennedy warehouse. The Metropolitan House hotel opened in summer 1857 (Pfaff pp. 40, 43-44).

t-pan-dells-dam.st: The Dells dam fight ran 26 years (1859-1885). It was approved in 1876 as part of a city waterworks, with $100,000 in bonds passed 808 to 12, and built by the Eau Claire Dells Improvement Co. from February 1876 to 1879, making Dells Pond the largest log sorting works in Eau Claire, with a flume to send logs down to Half Moon Lake. The 1880 flood overflowed Dells Pond, "mowing down trees as if they had been grass" (Pfaff pp. 46-48, 60).
src: Pfaff, Settlement and Survival: Building Towns in the Chippewa Valley 1850-1925 (Chippewa Valley Museum, 1994), your screenshots

pb13-drywood.st: A Bohemian (Czech) settlement: the Cypreansen Brothers of Eau Claire hired agent Vincent Benesh to advertise their land in Bohemian papers, and by 1905 more than 100 families had settled around Drywood near Cadott. Their lodge was Brothers of the New Castle of the Western Bohemian Fraternal Association (ZCBJ), photographed in 1907 (Pfaff pp. 90-92). The lodge hall and dance grounds are good gathering spots: look for the ZCBJ hall on the 1913 plat.

sf-eau-claire-eagle-brewery-mrs-t-leinen.st: At the Saengerfest of 5 June 1870, the Chippewa Falls Saengerbund marched "to the west side beer garden, kept by Henry Leinenkugel & Son" (Eau Claire Weekly Free Press, 9 June 1870, in Pfaff p. 66).
